intro: Leaks have a way of hiding in plain sight — a slightly higher water bill, a damp patch behind a cupboard, or the faint sound of running water when everything's turned off. In Aberdeen, where cold winters and ageing pipe networks are facts of life, undetected leaks can cause serious damage before anyone notices. Whether it's a slow drip behind a bathroom wall or a more urgent burst, getting a leak found and fixed quickly saves you money, protects your home, and prevents the kind of damp damage that takes months and serious cash to put right. A qualified local plumber can locate and repair most leaks in a single visit.
localContext: Aberdeen's housing stock is genuinely varied, and that variety matters when it comes to leaks. The city has a large number of Victorian granite tenements and terraced properties — impressive buildings, but ones where original lead or iron pipework is sometimes still in service. These older pipes are more prone to corrosion, joint failures, and pinhole leaks that develop quietly over years. Post-war council and private housing across areas like Mastrick, Northfield, and Kincorth tends to have copper or early plastic pipework that's now reaching middle age and showing signs of wear. Newer developments in the likes of Westhill and Portlethen — though technically Greater Aberdeen — use modern plastic systems that are generally more reliable but not immune to installer errors or joint failures. Aberdeen sits in a moderately hard water area, which means some scale build-up in pipes over time. While it's not as aggressive as in the south of England, limescale can still narrow pipe bore and put extra stress on joints and valves, making leaks more likely in older installations.
serviceDetail: When you call out a plumber for leak detection in Aberdeen, the first thing they'll do is talk you through what you've noticed — the signs, how long it's been happening, and where in the property it seems to be coming from. That conversation alone often narrows things down significantly. From there, the plumber will carry out a visual inspection of accessible pipework, checking joints, valves, and any visible sections of pipe for moisture, corrosion, or staining. If the leak isn't immediately obvious, they'll use more targeted methods. Acoustic listening devices can pick up the sound of water escaping through a pipe even when it's buried under flooring or behind plasterwork. Thermal imaging cameras are another option — they detect temperature differences caused by water, making hidden leaks visible without lifting a single floorboard. Tracer gas testing, where a harmless gas is introduced into the pipework and detected at the surface, is used for more stubborn cases. Once the source is confirmed, the repair itself is usually straightforward — cutting out a damaged section, replacing a joint, or resealing a connection. Most jobs in Aberdeen homes are completed in two to four hours, and in the majority of cases there's no need for major disruption to floors, walls, or ceilings. You'll be given a clear explanation of what was found and what was done before the plumber leaves.
pricing: In Aberdeen, most leak detection and repair jobs fall in the range of £100 to £500, depending on how complex the job turns out to be. A straightforward accessible leak — say, under a kitchen sink or at a visible joint — might come in at £100 to £150 including labour and parts. If the leak requires specialist detection equipment like thermal imaging or acoustic devices, expect to add £75 to £150 for that element. Leaks hidden beneath concrete floors or behind tiled walls will cost more, both for detection and repair, typically sitting in the £250 to £500 range. Call-out charges in Aberdeen generally range from £50 to £80 for standard hours, with emergency or out-of-hours work priced higher. Always ask for a clear quote before work begins.
whyLocal: Choosing a plumber based in Aberdeen rather than a national firm makes a real difference on a leak job. Local tradespeople know the area's housing stock — they've worked in granite tenements, 1960s semis, and new-builds, and they understand the quirks of each. They're also familiar with the water infrastructure across Aberdeen's different neighbourhoods, which can affect how leaks behave and how quickly they can be traced. Response times are faster, there's no middleman taking a cut, and you're dealing with someone who has a local reputation to protect. For something as time-sensitive as a leak, that local knowledge and accountability genuinely counts.

faqs.q: How do I know if I have a hidden leak in my Aberdeen home?
faqs.a: Common signs include an unexplained rise in your water bill, the sound of running water when everything's turned off, damp patches on walls or ceilings, or a drop in water pressure. In older Aberdeen properties, discolouration on plaster or skirting boards is often the first visible clue. If you notice any of these, it's worth getting a plumber to check — catching it early is always cheaper.

faqs.q: Will the plumber need to dig up my floors to find the leak?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Modern leak detection equipment — including acoustic devices and thermal imaging cameras — can often pinpoint a leak without any digging or lifting. In many Aberdeen homes, the source is identified and repaired with minimal disruption. If excavation is needed, the plumber should explain exactly why and what's involved before proceeding.

faqs.q: Can hard water cause leaks in Aberdeen properties?
faqs.a: Aberdeen is a moderately hard water area, so while it's not extreme, scale build-up does occur over time — particularly in older copper pipework. Limescale can narrow joints and cause corrosion that eventually leads to pinhole leaks. It's one reason why ageing pipe systems in Victorian and post-war Aberdeen properties are worth keeping an eye on, especially at elbows and connections.

faqs.q: How quickly can a plumber respond to a leak in Aberdeen?
faqs.a: Most local Aberdeen plumbers offer same-day response for urgent leaks, and many provide an emergency call-out service for out-of-hours situations. If you've already isolated the water supply and the situation is contained, a next-day appointment is usually sufficient. For active leaks causing damage, turn off your stop valve first and call immediately — most plumbers will prioritise accordingly.
